title: Broken Windows Theory And Classroom Management nagement/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin summarizes Malcolm Gladwell's account, in The Tipping Point, of New York City's crime drop in the 1990s, attributing much of it to the 'broken windows theory' -- the idea that visible disorder signals that no one is watching or in charge, inviting more serious crime, and that cleaning up minor infractions like graffiti and fare-jumping produced outsized reductions in overall crime. He applies this directly to classroom management using the image of a messy row of student backpacks, arguing that tolerating small signs of disorder and disrespect sends the same 'no one is watching' signal to students and invites more serious disruptive behavior. He argues teachers commonly wait until a rule is broken 'in a big way' before enforcing it, which creates a confusing sliding scale of enforcement dependent on mood or the identity of the student, and that this inconsistency itself invites students to test limits further. Using an example of a well-behaved student calling out a question without raising her hand, he insists that enforcing rules precisely and impartially -- even with 'good' students, even over trivial infractions -- is what actually prevents larger behavior problems. The piece closes with a direct challenge to test the broken windows theory by enforcing even minor classroom infractions consistently.
points: Malcolm Gladwell's 'broken windows theory' of crime reduction is applied to classroom management: small visible signs of disorder invite larger, more frequent misbehavior.
A messy row of student backpacks is used as an illustration of how tolerating minor disorder signals that standards of respect and care are not truly valued.
Waiting to enforce a rule until it's broken 'in a big way' creates a confusing, inconsistent sliding scale of enforcement that invites students to test limits.
Even well-behaved students breaking minor rules (e.g., calling out without raising a hand) should be held to the same standard, since selective enforcement undermines the whole plan.
The core prescription is to enforce even minor, seemingly inconsequential classroom management rules precisely and consistently, without exception.
quotes: The broken windows theory of crime prevention postulates that disorder is an invitation for crime to occur. If the environment of a particular neighborhood triggers the belief that no one cares or that no one is in charge, then crime in that neighborhood goes up.

Just as enforcing minor quality-of-life crimes can benefit cities and neighborhoods, enforcing classroom rule violations that many teachers perceive to be not worth the time are, in fact, very much worth the time.
Small details that for many teachers don’t seem to be worth the effort can have a strong impact on the behavior of your students.

Too many teachers wait until a rule is broken in a big way before enforcing it. This is a mistake in the highest order. It’s confusing to students to have rules on a sliding scale, dependent upon your mood, who the student is, or how severely the rule was broken.

The fact is, this is a wonderful opportunity. That the student is one of your best is perfect. It’s an opportunity to show all of your students that rules will be enforced no matter what, no matter when, and no matter who is breaking them.
Test the broken windows theory in your own classroom by enforcing even the little things—minor infractions that at first seem inconsequential, but in reality, are the most important.
